verifiedClaims.claim: Every year, tens of thousands of car accidents happen on South Carolina roads.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina recorded 143,801 traffic collisions in 2024 (1,040 people killed, 51,007 non-fatal injuries) — one collision every 3.7 minutes, one person killed every 8.4 hours. 2023: 145,761 collisions; 2022: 143,426.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS, South Carolina Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition, p. 3 (Traffic Collisions, Fatalities, Non-Fatal Injuries 1985–2024) and Collision Statistics Clock
verifiedClaims.note: 'Tens of thousands' understates by an order of magnitude. Suggested: 'More than 140,000 traffic collisions happen on South Carolina roads every year — 143,801 in 2024, killing 1,040 people and injuring 51,007 more, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Safety's Traffic Collision Fact Book.'

verifiedClaims.claim: According to the South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles, the state processes hundreds of thousands of collision reports annually
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The annual collision count is published by the South Carolina Department of Public Safety, not SCDMV, and it is 143,801 (2024) — not 'hundreds of thousands'. SCDMV is the custodian of the TR-310 collision reports (officers forward them to SCDMV under § 56-5-1270) but publishes no annual count. The linked host scdmvonline.com now redirects to dmv.sc.gov.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Fact Book 2024, p. 3; S.C. Code § 56-5-1270; SCDMV Collision Reports page
verifiedClaims.note: Wrong agency and wrong magnitude. Fold into the corrected first sentence (SCDPS Fact Book) and drop the SCDMV attribution and its homepage link, or repoint the link to https://dmv.sc.gov/Vehicle-Owners/Collision-Reports where the TR-310 is actually requested.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina is an at-fault state, meaning the driver who caused the accident bears financial responsibility for injuries and property damage.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 38-77-140 (mandatory liability policy 'against loss from the liability imposed by law'); Title 38, Chapter 77 contains no personal-injury-protection or no-fault requirement
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. South Carolina has no PIP requirement and no no-fault system; the post never says otherwise. The table cell 'At-fault (tort) state' is the same fact.

verifiedClaims.claim: You have three years to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530
verifiedClaims.note: § 15-3-530(5): three years for 'any injury to the person or rights of another, not arising on contract'. Matches the writer-profile table. Repeated correctly in the table cell, the Three-Year Statute of Limitations H3, the 'Waiting Too Long' section, keyTakeaways and faq:1. Optional add (writer-profile row): two years under § 15-78-110 if the defendant is a state or local government entity.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina also requires all auto insurance policies to include uninsured motorist (UM) coverage under S.C. Code § 38-77-150, which provides a safety net when the at-fault driver has no insurance or not enough coverage.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: UM coverage (§ 38-77-150) is mandatory and pays what the insured is 'legally entitled to recover as damages from the owner or operator of an uninsured motor vehicle'. The 'not enough coverage' case is underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage under § 38-77-160, which insurers must offer 'at the option of the insured' — it is optional, not required.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: '... uninsured motorist (UM) coverage under S.C. Code § 38-77-150, a safety net when the at-fault driver has no insurance; underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage, which insurers must offer under § 38-77-160, covers the driver who has too little.' The same UM/UIM conflation recurs in the At-Fault State paragraph and the Mandatory UM section.

verifiedClaims.claim: Whether your accident happened on I-26 in Charleston, I-77 in Columbia, or Highway 17 along the Grand Strand, the same legal principles apply.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/firm-facts.md (office corridors: Charleston I-26/I-526/US-17; Columbia I-20/I-26/I-77; Myrtle Beach US-17/SC-31/US-501)
verifiedClaims.note: Geography matches the firm record's corridors. No figure asserted.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under S.C. Code § 56-5-1210, every driver involved in an accident that causes injury, death, or property damage must immediately stop at the scene or as close to it as safely possible.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 56-5-1210(A) covers accidents 'resulting in injury to or the death of a person'. Damage-only crashes are governed by § 56-5-1220 (attended vehicle — stop, remain, and if the vehicle is drivable and obstructing traffic, 'make every reasonable effort to move' it off the roadway) and § 56-5-1240 (unattended vehicle). All three require the driver to remain until the § 56-5-1230 duties (identify yourself, show your license on request, render reasonable aid) are met.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Under S.C. Code § 56-5-1210, every driver involved in an accident that causes injury or death must immediately stop at the scene or as close to it as safely possible; § 56-5-1220 imposes the same duty when only vehicles are damaged.' Also fix 'stay put' in the next sentence — see the fender-bender entry.

verifiedClaims.claim: Leaving the scene of an accident involving injuries is a felony in South Carolina, punishable by up to 25 years in prison if someone dies.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Under § 56-5-1210(A), leaving the scene is (1) a misdemeanor — 30 days to one year and/or $100–$5,000 — 'when injury results but great bodily injury or death does not result'; (2) a felony, 30 days to ten years and $5,000–$10,000, when great bodily injury results; (3) a felony, one to twenty-five years and $10,000–$25,000, when death results. SCDMV revokes the license on any conviction ((D)).
verifiedClaims.note: Same error class corrected in the Surfside DUI post (run-4729) on 2026-09-24. Suggested: 'Leaving the scene of an injury crash is a crime in South Carolina — a misdemeanor when someone is hurt, and a felony carrying up to ten years when it causes great bodily injury or one to 25 years when someone dies.' The '25 years' figure is right; the blanket 'felony' is not.

verifiedClaims.claim: Even in a fender-bender, pull over safely and stay put.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 56-5-1220(B): if a vehicle involved in a damage-only accident 'is obstructing traffic, the driver of the vehicle shall make every reasonable effort to move any vehicle that is capable of being driven safely off the roadway', and a driver who does so before police arrive 'shall not be considered liable or at fault ... solely by reason of moving the vehicle'.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Stay put' reads as 'leave the car where it is', which the statute reverses for drivable cars blocking traffic. Suggested: 'Even in a fender-bender, stay at the scene — but if your car can be driven and is blocking traffic, South Carolina law tells you to move it out of the roadway first (§ 56-5-1220), and doing so cannot be held against you.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, law enforcement will respond to any accident involving injuries or significant property damage.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No statute guarantees a police response. What the law requires is the reverse: the driver in an injury or death crash must 'immediately by the quickest means of communication' notify the local police (inside a municipality) or the sheriff or nearest Highway Patrol office (§ 56-5-1260). If no officer investigates and the crash caused injury, death or apparent property damage of $1,000 or more, the driver or owner must file a written report with proof of insurance (SCDMV Form FR-309) with SCDMV within 15 days, and failing to do so is prima facie evidence the vehicle was uninsured (§ 56-5-1270). SCDPS: 'SCHP cannot investigate collisions that were not reported to law enforcement after the incident.'
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1260, 56-5-1270; SCDPS Resources (Collision and Towing Questions)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'South Carolina law requires you to report any crash involving injury or death to police immediately (S.C. Code § 56-5-1260). If no officer investigates a crash that caused injury, death or $1,000 or more in damage, you must file your own report (SCDMV Form FR-309) with proof of insurance within 15 days (§ 56-5-1270) — skip it and the law presumes your car was uninsured.' Note § 56-5-1260 itself covers injury/death only; the $1,000 threshold belongs to § 56-5-1270.

verifiedClaims.claim: The responding officer will file an FR-10 collision report, which becomes a critical piece of evidence in your claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The officer's collision report is the TR-310, forwarded to SCDMV within 24 hours of completing the investigation (§ 56-5-1270). The FR-10 is the 'mandatory insurance verification form' the officer hands each driver at the scene (SCDPS: 'If you lost your FR10 (mandatory insurance verification form), please contact the appropriate troop office'). Under § 56-5-1290, none of the required reports 'may be evidence of the negligence or due care of either party at the trial of any action at law to recover damages', though officers may use them to refresh recollection when testifying.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Resources; S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1270, 56-5-1290; SCDPS TR-310 Report Manual (rev. May 2019)
verifiedClaims.note: Wrong form, published three times (here, the H3 'Obtain the FR-10 Police Report', and its paragraph). Suggested: 'The responding officer files a TR-310 collision report with the SCDMV and hands you an FR-10 insurance-verification form — keep it. The TR-310 is what adjusters work from, even though the report itself cannot be used at trial to prove who was negligent (§ 56-5-1290).' Same finding as runs 1740 and 4711.

verifiedClaims.claim: Collect the following from every other driver involved: Full name and contact information; Driver's license number; Insurance company and policy number; Vehicle make, model, year, and license plate number
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-1230 (driver must give name, address and registration number, and exhibit a driver's license on request)
verifiedClaims.note: The list is the practical superset of the statutory duty. Optional: cite § 56-5-1230, which also imposes the duty to render reasonable aid.

verifiedClaims.claim: Even if you feel fine, see a doctor within 24 hours. Many serious injuries, including traumatic brain injuries, whiplash, and internal bleeding, do not produce immediate symptoms.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: CDC HEADS UP — Concussion Signs and Symptoms ('may take hours or days to appear or be noticed'), verified in run-4711
verifiedClaims.note: 'Within 24 hours' is the firm's advice, not a medical finding; the delayed-symptom premise is CDC-supported. No change.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina law requires you to notify your own insurance company of an accident promptly.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No South Carolina statute requires a policyholder to notify the insurer; the duty comes from the policy's notice and cooperation conditions, which the post's next sentence already describes. The statutory reporting duties run to the police (§ 56-5-1260) and, when no officer investigates, to SCDMV within 15 days (§ 56-5-1270).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1260, 56-5-1270; Title 38, Chapter 77 (no policyholder-notice statute)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Your auto policy almost certainly requires you to notify your insurer of an accident promptly — the notice and cooperation conditions are in every standard policy — and that is true even when the other driver was at fault.' Delete 'South Carolina law requires'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina uses the FR-10 form for all traffic collision reports. You can request a copy from the law enforcement agency that responded to the accident or through the South Carolina Department of Public Safety.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The collision report is the TR-310. SCDPS directs requests to SCDMV: 'If you are involved in a collision and wish to obtain a copy of the collision report (TR-310), you may request it through the South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles.' SCDMV: request online, or with Request for Copy of Collision Report (SCDMV Form FR-50) at any branch or by mail, $10 per report; 'The collision report is more detailed than the report you received the day of the collision.' A person named in the report may also obtain it from the investigating agency (§ 56-5-1275).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Resources; SCDMV — Collision Reports; S.C. Code § 56-5-1275
verifiedClaims.note: Retitle the H3 'Obtain the TR-310 Collision Report'. Suggested: 'South Carolina officers file collision reports on Form TR-310, which goes to the SCDMV. Request a copy from SCDMV online or with Form FR-50 ($10), or from the police department that responded. The FR-10 you were handed at the scene is only the insurance-verification form.' FR-50 PDF: https://dmv.sc.gov/sites/scdmv/files/2026-01/FR-50%20Request%20for%20Copy%20of%20Collision%20Report.pdf

verifiedClaims.claim: This report contains the officer's narrative, a diagram of the collision, witness information, and any citations issued. Review it carefully for errors, since mistakes in police reports are more common than you might think.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1270 (report must include names of interviewed participants and witnesses), 56-5-1300 (forms must disclose 'the cause, conditions then existing and the persons and vehicles involved'); SCDPS TR-310 Report Manual
verifiedClaims.note: Content description holds for the TR-310. 'More common than you might think' is unsourced rhetoric; harmless, but optional to trim.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's car accident laws differ from neighboring states in several important ways. If you are from Georgia or have been in accidents in other states, do not assume the same rules apply here.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md — 'Cross-jurisdiction law on a single-state page is an error'
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia mention 1 of 9. Drop the Georgia clause; the section can open 'South Carolina's car accident laws differ from other states' in several important ways.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia (for comparison) ... At-fault (tort) state ... 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) ... Less than 50% at fault to recover ... Optional (offered, not required) ... 25/50/25 ... $250K statutory cap (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Remove the Georgia column and retitle the table 'South Carolina Car Accident Laws at a Glance'. For the record: § 9-3-33 (two years), § 51-12-33(g) (no recovery at 50% or more) and § 51-12-5.1(g) ($250,000 cap, lifted for impaired drivers under (f)) were verified in runs 1740/1722; the Georgia UM and minimum-limits cells were not re-verified this run (Justia 403; search budget exhausted).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md jurisdiction rules; runs 1740 and 1722 for the three verified Georgia cells
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia mentions 2–3 of 9 (header plus the column). A two-column table (Legal Issue / South Carolina) keeps every SC cell and all its internal anchors. Do not carry any O.C.G.A. citation into the SC-only post.

verifiedClaims.claim: 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
verifiedClaims.note: Table cell.

verifiedClaims.claim: Less than 51% at fault to recover
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991) — plaintiff recovers if his or her negligence is 'not greater than' the defendant's
verifiedClaims.note: Table cell. Correct; a plaintiff exactly 50% at fault still recovers. Attribute to Nelson if a citation is added — never § 15-38-15 (writer-profile rule).

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes (S.C. Code § 38-77-150)
verifiedClaims.note: Table cell (Mandatory UM Coverage). Correct.

verifiedClaims.currentValue: $25,000 bodily injury per person / $50,000 bodily injury per accident / $25,000 property damage per accident
verifiedClaims.note: Table cell (South Carolina). Correct; optional citation § 38-77-140.

verifiedClaims.claim: Greater of 3x compensatory or $500K (S.C. Code § 15-32-530)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (§ 15-32-530(A)), but the dollar floor is CPI-indexed under (D): the S.C. Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office memo of 2026-02-03 sets the 2026 limit at $739,245 (2025: $719,971). The cap rises to the greater of 4x or $2,000,000 under (B) and disappears entirely under (C), including where 'the defendant acted or failed to act while under the influence of alcohol, drugs ... to the degree that the defendant's judgment is substantially impaired'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-32-530(A)-(D); S.C. Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office, 'Punitive Damage Award Limitation – Inflation Component', memo of February 3, 2026
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested cell: 'Greater of 3x compensatory or $500K, indexed — $739,245 in 2026; no cap for drunk drivers (S.C. Code § 15-32-530)'. Same correction in the Punitive Damages paragraph, keyTakeaways and faq:4.

verifiedClaims.claim: You can pursue compensation by filing a claim with the at-fault driver's insurance company (a third-party claim), filing a lawsuit against the at-fault driver, or using your own UM coverage if the at-fault driver is uninsured or underinsured.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: UM (§ 38-77-150) applies to an uninsured driver; the underinsured case is UIM (§ 38-77-160), optional coverage the insurer must offer.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: '... or using your own UM coverage if the at-fault driver is uninsured — or UIM coverage, if you bought it, when the driver's limits are too low.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Miss that deadline and the court will almost certainly dismiss your case. Three years sounds like plenty of time, but medical treatment, negotiations with insurance companies, and gathering evidence can consume months.
verifiedClaims.note: Characterization consistent with the limitations bar. No change.

verifiedClaims.claim: For comparison, Georgia's statute of limitations is only two years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. If your accident happened near the state line, confirming which state's laws apply is critical.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md jurisdiction rules (single-state page); O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 verified in run 1740
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia mention 4 of 9. The two-year figure is accurate but belongs on the Georgia guide. Delete the paragraph; if a border line is wanted, 'If your crash happened in another state, that state's deadline may be shorter — confirm it early' says it without importing Georgia law.

verifiedClaims.claim: Every auto insurance policy sold in South Carolina must include UM coverage unless the policyholder specifically rejects it in writing.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: There is no rejection option. § 38-77-150(A): 'No automobile insurance policy or contract may be issued or delivered unless it contains a provision ... undertaking to pay the insured all sums which he is legally entitled to recover as damages from the owner or operator of an uninsured motor vehicle, within limits which may be no less than the requirements of Section 38-77-140.' What the insured may decline is the optional additional UM above the minimums and UIM, both offered 'at the option of the insured' under § 38-77-160.
verifiedClaims.note: The 'reject in writing' mechanism is Georgia's, not South Carolina's — a cross-jurisdiction leak on the very rule the section calls South Carolina's most significant difference. Suggested: 'Every auto policy issued in South Carolina must include UM coverage of at least 25/50/25 — a policyholder cannot waive it. Higher UM limits and underinsured (UIM) coverage must be offered, but those are optional (§ 38-77-160).'

verifiedClaims.claim: This coverage protects you when the at-fault driver has no insurance or insufficient coverage, which happens more often than you would expect. Roughly one in eight South Carolina drivers is uninsured.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Insurance Research Council, 'Uninsured and Underinsured Motorists: 2017 to 2023' (Feb. 20, 2025), as republished by the Insurance Information Institute: 10.3% of South Carolina motorists were uninsured in 2023 (39th among the states); the national rate was 15.4% ('more than one in seven'); Mississippi highest at 28.2%, Maine lowest at 5.7%.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Insurance Research Council (IRC), Uninsured and Underinsured Motorists: 2017–2023, via Insurance Information Institute, 'Facts + Statistics: Uninsured motorists'
verifiedClaims.note: 'One in eight' (12.5%) overstates; the current estimate is about one in ten. Suggested: 'This coverage protects you when the at-fault driver has no insurance — about one in ten South Carolina drivers (10.3% in 2023, according to the Insurance Research Council). Underinsured (UIM) coverage, if you bought it, covers the driver whose limits are too low.' The IRC full report is paywalled; the III page carries the IRC state table and is the citable public copy.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina requires all drivers to carry minimum liability insurance of 25/50/25: $25,000 per person for bodily injury, $50,000 per accident for bodily injury, and $25,000 per accident for property damage.
verifiedClaims.note: Figures verified verbatim ('twenty-five thousand dollars because of bodily injury to one person', 'fifty thousand dollars ... two or more persons', 'twenty-five thousand dollars because of injury to or destruction of property'). Nuance not worth adding: § 38-77-150(C) references an option 'to be uninsured by paying the fee pursuant to Section 56-10-510'; that fee was not verified this run.

verifiedClaims.claim: These minimums are often insufficient to cover serious injury claims. A single hospital stay after a truck accident or multi-vehicle collision can easily exceed $25,000.
verifiedClaims.note: Hypothetical illustration tied to the verified $25,000 per-person limit; no settlement or verdict figure asserted. Keep.

verifiedClaims.claim: A demand letter to the at-fault driver's insurance company outlines the facts of the accident, your injuries, your damages, and the amount you are seeking. This opens formal negotiations.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 38, Chapter 59 (no demand statute; § 38-59-20(2) requires insurers to acknowledge claim communications 'with reasonable promptness', enforced by the Director of Insurance) — verified in run 1722
verifiedClaims.note: The post asserts no response deadline and no statute, which is correct for South Carolina. Do not add one: the only statutory duty on the other driver's insurer is 'reasonable promptness' under § 38-59-20, and the 90-day § 38-59-40 remedy is first-party only.

verifiedClaims.claim: The insurer will respond with a counteroffer, usually far below what your claim is worth.
verifiedClaims.note: Characterization of practice with no figure or statute; 'usually' is unsourced but low-stakes. Optional soften: 'often'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Most personal injury cases settle before trial, but the willingness to go to court gives your attorney leverage during negotiations.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Same finding as run 1722 (demand-letter post): no primary source for the settlement-rate claim; data/statistics.json carries none
verifiedClaims.note: Replace 'Most personal injury cases settle before trial' with 'Many cases settle before trial' — no population statistic, no source needed.

verifiedClaims.claim: filing a lawsuit in South Carolina circuit court may be necessary
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SC Judicial Branch — circuit court (Court of Common Pleas hears civil actions); magistrates have concurrent jurisdiction to $7,500 (§ 22-3-10, verified in run 4729)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. Optional precision: 'the Court of Common Pleas (circuit court)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault system. If you were partially at fault for the accident, you can still recover damages, but only if your share of fault is less than 51 percent. If you are found 51 percent or more at fault, you recover nothing.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Rule correct. The post does not cite a source; if one is added it is Nelson, not § 15-38-15. Verified verbatim in runs 4729, 4711, 1740.

verifiedClaims.claim: if a jury awards you $100,000 in damages but finds you were 30 percent at fault (maybe you were slightly speeding while the other driver ran a red light), your award is reduced by 30 percent. You would receive $70,000.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (1991): recovery 'reduced in proportion to the amount of his or her negligence'
verifiedClaims.note: Hypothetical, clearly framed as such; arithmetic correct.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's threshold is slightly stricter: you must be less than 50 percent at fault to recover anything. If you were involved in a crash near the Georgia-South Carolina border, the state where the accident occurred determines which comparative fault rule applies.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md jurisdiction rules; O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g) verified in run 1740
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia mentions 5–6 of 9. The Georgia figure is accurate but out of scope; the choice-of-law sentence was not verified and is not needed. Delete the paragraph.

verifiedClaims.claim: Economic Damages ... Medical bills ... Lost wages and lost earning capacity ... Property damage ... Out-of-pocket expenses. Non-Economic Damages ... Pain and suffering; Emotional distress; Loss of enjoyment of life; Loss of consortium (impact on your relationship with your spouse); Scarring and disfigurement
verifiedClaims.sourceName: General South Carolina damages categories; no ordinary-negligence cap on economic or non-economic damages (Title 15, Chapter 32 caps only medical-malpractice non-economic damages, § 15-32-220, and punitive damages, § 15-32-530); Tort Claims Act cap $300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence (§ 15-78-120(a))
verifiedClaims.note: No figure asserted. The post correctly implies no general cap. Optional one-line add for completeness: 'There is no cap on these damages in an ordinary car-accident case; the exceptions are claims against a government entity ($300,000 per person under § 15-78-120) and medical malpractice.' Lost wages are taxable income when recovered for physical injury? No — per run 1769, lost-wage recoveries in a physical-injury case are excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2); the post makes no tax claim.

verifiedClaims.claim: In cases involving reckless, willful, or wanton conduct, such as drunk driving or extreme speeding, South Carolina allows punitive damages under S.C. Code § 15-32-530.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The standard is in § 15-32-520(D): punitive damages 'may be awarded only if the plaintiff proves by clear and convincing evidence that his harm was the result of the defendant's wilful, wanton, or reckless conduct'. § 15-32-530 is the cap statute — and its subsection (C)(3) removes the cap when the defendant was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs, so the post's own drunk-driving example is the one case the stated cap does not govern.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'In cases involving wilful, wanton or reckless conduct, such as drunk driving or extreme speeding, South Carolina allows punitive damages (S.C. Code §§ 15-32-520 and 15-32-530).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Punitive damages in South Carolina are capped at the greater of three times the compensatory damages or $500,000.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Greater of 3x compensatory or $500,000 under § 15-32-530(A), with the dollar floor indexed to CPI each year under (D) — $739,245 for 2026 per the RFA memo of February 3, 2026 (cumulative 47.8% since December 2010). Higher tier of 4x or $2,000,000 under (B) (conduct motivated by unreasonable financial gain known to management, or felony-level conduct). No cap under (C): intent to harm, a felony plea or conviction arising from the same conduct, or a defendant whose judgment was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-32-530; S.C. Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office memo, 'Punitive Damage Award Limitation – Inflation Component', Feb. 3, 2026
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Punitive damages are normally capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or a dollar floor indexed for inflation each year — $739,245 in 2026. The cap rises to four times or $2 million for felony-level conduct, and there is no cap at all when the defendant was drunk or drugged to the point of substantial impairment (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).' Same figure in keyTakeaways and faq:4; also the table cell.

verifiedClaims.claim: The plaintiff must prove entitlement to punitive damages by clear and convincing evidence, a higher standard than the preponderance standard used for other damages.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim. Optional: cite § 15-32-520.

verifiedClaims.claim: The at-fault driver's insurance company will call you and ask for a recorded statement. You are not legally required to provide one.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: No South Carolina statute or Title 38 provision obliges a third-party claimant to give a statement to the other driver's insurer; the cooperation duty runs only to one's own insurer under the policy
verifiedClaims.note: Correct as to the at-fault driver's carrier. The post's earlier advice to keep the statement to one's own insurer 'brief and factual' is consistent with the policy cooperation clause. No change.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your policy may include medical payments coverage (MedPay), which pays your medical bills regardless of fault, in addition to the mandatory UM coverage.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 38, Chapter 77 — MedPay is not a required coverage; the post says 'may include'
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate hedge. South Carolina has no PIP requirement; do not let a refresh turn MedPay into 'PIP' or 'no-fault benefits'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Personal injury attorneys in South Carolina work on a contingency fee basis, meaning you pay nothing upfront and no attorney fees unless your case results in compensation.

verifiedClaims.claim: After a SC accident: call 911, document scene, do not admit fault. SC requires stopping (S.C. Code § 56-5-1210). 3-year SOL (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Mandatory UM coverage (S.C. Code § 38-77-150). Comparative fault bars at 51%. Min insurance 25/50/25. Punitive capped at 3x or $500K (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Every element verified except the punitive figure: the $500K floor is indexed and stands at $739,245 for 2026 (RFA memo 2026-02-03), and § 15-32-530(C)(3) removes the cap for a substantially impaired driver. § 56-5-1210 requires stopping at injury and death crashes (§ 56-5-1220 for damage-only).
verifiedClaims.note: Renders in the summary box above the article. statuteCitations.name: Duties of drivers involved in accident resulting in death or personal injury — misdemeanor when injury only; felony (30 days–10 years) for great bodily injury; felony (1–25 years) for death; license revocation

Duties of driver involved in accident resulting in damage to attended vehicles — stop and remain; move a drivable vehicle off the roadway if obstructing traffic, without that being held against the driver
Duty to give information (name, address, registration number; license on request) and render reasonable aid
Immediate report of accidents resulting in personal injury or death — to local police, sheriff or nearest Highway Patrol office by the quickest means

Written reports — driver/owner files with SCDMV within 15 days (Form FR-309, with insurance verification) when no officer investigates and there is injury, death or $1,000+ damage; investigating officer forwards the report (TR-310) to SCDMV within 24 hours; failure to file is prima facie evidence the vehicle was uninsured
Requests for accident investigation reports — persons named in the report may obtain it from the agency; no release for commercial solicitation
Evidentiary use of reports — the required reports may not be evidence of negligence or due care at trial; officers may use them to refresh recollection
Reports made by persons involved are without prejudice and confidential; not usable as evidence in any trial
Minimum liability limits — $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident bodily injury / $25,000 property damage
Uninsured motorist provision — mandatory on every policy at no less than the § 38-77-140 limits; no waiver
Additional UM and underinsured motorist coverage — must be offered at the insured's option up to the liability limits; stacking limited to the coverage on the vehicle involved
Conditions to recover UM when the at-fault driver is unknown — prompt police report plus physical contact, an independent witness affidavit, or a recording
Improper claim practices — insurers must acknowledge claim communications with reasonable promptness; regulator-enforced; no statutory deadline to answer a third-party demand
Three years — (5) injury to the person; (6) wrongful death, running from the death
Tort Claims Act statute of limitations — two years from discovery of the loss; three if a verified claim was first filed
Tort Claims Act limits — $300,000 per person, $600,000 per occurrence; no punitive damages
Punitive damages — bifurcated trial; clear and convincing evidence of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (D)

Punitive damages cap — greater of 3x compensatory or $500,000, CPI-indexed under (D) ($739,245 for 2026); 4x or $2,000,000 under (B); no cap under (C) including substantial impairment by alcohol or drugs
Medical-malpractice non-economic damages cap ($350,000 per provider / $1,050,000 total, CPI-indexed) — the only non-economic cap outside the Tort Claims Act; not cited in the post
Apportionment among defendants responsible for less than 50% of fault — never cite for the plaintiff's comparative-fault bar (that is Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.)
